title: You can control *everything,* but *not the right time.*
description: Some projects arrive exactly when you expect them to. Others take their time. The rebranding of Salad Days belonged firmly in the second category.

blocks.heading: Some projects arrive exactly when you expect them to. Others take their time. The rebranding of Salad Days belonged firmly in the *second category.*
SOME CONVERSATIONS TAKE LONGER

Long before there was a formal brief, there was a *friendship.* Over the course of more than <ref n="01"/> three years, countless conversations revolved around the brand, what it stood for, how people perceived it, and where it could go next. Every now and then those conversations turned into small collaborations, but the larger question of reimagining the brand always remained somewhere in the background.

annotations.text: The work started years before the timeline did.

blocks.heading: A BRAND PEOPLE ALREADY LOVED
So when the opportunity finally arrived, it didn't feel like the beginning of a new project. It felt like the continuation<ref n="02"/> of a conversation that had been unfolding for years.

annotations.text: Meaningful creative work often begins long before a contract is signed, taking shape through conversations, observations, shared experiences, and accumulated understanding.

blocks.leftColumn: *One thing became clear almost immediately: this wasn't a brand that needed reinvention.*
blocks.rightColumn: Salad Days had already established a meaningful place in the lives of its customers. It had built recognition, familiarity, and a distinct personality over time. The challenge wasn't to create something entirely new, but to understand what people already connected with and strengthen those foundations for the future.

blocks.heading: A TEAL QUESTION

Like many rebranding projects, the process began by identifying the elements that carried the strongest memory value. Interestingly, one particular element kept resurfacing.

The *Teal.*

Whether we were reviewing past communication, discussing customer recall, or imagining future applications, the colour consistently found its way back into the conversation. It had become one of the brand's most recognizable assets—not because it was loud or distinctive in isolation, but because it had quietly earned its place over years of consistent use.

*The question was never whether it should remain. The question was whether it was the right teal.*
GROWTH NEEDS A BIGGER PALETTE

As the brand evolved, the existing colour no longer felt capable of carrying the growing ambitions of the business. We needed something with greater confidence and presence—something that could unify packaging, digital communication, retail environments, and future extensions of the brand without losing the familiarity people already associated with Salad Days.

The answer wasn't replacement. It was refinement.

While the teal remained at the center of the identity, the broader colour system required a more significant evolution.
DESIGNING FOR FLEXIBILITY

Consumer brands live across an enormous range of touchpoints. Menus, packaging, social media, campaigns, merchandise, seasonal launches, and promotional materials all compete for attention. *Relying* too *heavily* on *a single colour* can eventually create repetition rather than recognition.

The challenge was to build a system that felt *cohesive* without becoming predictable.

By introducing a complementary palette, we created a framework that allowed the brand to communicate with greater flexibility while maintaining a consistent visual voice. The objective wasn't variety for the sake of variety. It was creating a system capable of growing alongside the brand.

With the colour direction beginning to take shape, our attention turned toward the *logotype.*
FINDING A FORM

While the existing identity had a logotype, it did not have a dedicated symbol.

That works for many brands, but as we explored the future of Salad Days, it became clear that the brand needed a form that could communicate alongside the wordmark. A strong symbol creates memory in a different way. It can live independently, become a visual shorthand, and build recognition across multiple touchpoints.

blocks.leftColumn: The challenge was finding a form that wasn't merely decorative or directly representational. We wanted something that could connect to the broader lifestyle and values associated with the brand.
blocks.rightColumn: After extensive exploration, we found inspiration in the unique fruit, flower, and seed form of the Indian Shaal tree (Shorea robusta). What attracted us was its ability to hold multiple meanings simultaneously.

blocks.heading:
The form is dynamic and organic. It references *nature, growth, and nourishment.* At the same time, it subtly resembles a human figure seated in meditation, reflecting balance, mindfulness, and well-being. Within its construction emerged a droplet-like negative space, almost resembling a nectar or essence held within the form.

The result is a *symbol that feels rooted yet contemporary.* It provides a strong anchor for the visual language and expands the brand's ability to communicate without relying solely on words.
WHEN RECOGNITION ISN'T THE PROBLEM

For a moment, we assumed this would be where most of the work lived.

After all, logos tend to become the centerpiece of any rebranding conversation. Yet the deeper we looked, the more we realized that *recognition was not the problem.* The existing mark already carried equity. People knew it. They trusted it. They associated it with the brand.

What it needed was *refinement.*

blocks.leftColumn: *Over the last decade, simplification has become a dominant trend in identity design. In many cases, that approach makes perfect sense.*
blocks.rightColumn:
But Salad Days is not a technology platform or a purely functional service. It is a brand built around \*habits, routines, choices, and a lifestyle \*people actively choose to participate in.

That relationship called for *warmth.*

It called for *character.*

And it called for a little more personality than extreme simplification would allow.

The modifications themselves were subtle. Most customers will likely never notice them consciously. Yet branding often operates in that space between observation and feeling. Small adjustments to proportion, rhythm, and form can influence perception long before someone understands why.

blocks.heading:
Those are often the most satisfying changes to make.

As rewarding as the strategic work was, the most enjoyable part of the project emerged elsewhere.

The *illustration* system.
BEYOND PHOTOGRAPHY

Salad Days has long taken a different approach from many contemporary food brands. Rather than relying heavily on photography, much of its communication is built through illustration. This creates an interesting challenge. Photography naturally communicates freshness, texture, and appetite.

*Illustrations have to work much harder to achieve the same effect. At the same time, that challenge presented an opportunity.*

*If executed thoughtfully, illustration could become one of the brand's most distinctive assets.*

The inspiration came from the ingredients themselves—things that are grown, nurtured, harvested, and thoughtfully prepared. We began exploring a visual language that felt similarly organic. Rather than developing a collection of standalone graphics, the goal was to create a living system that could continuously expand alongside the brand.

*Ingredients became characters.*

*Shapes became building blocks.*

Individual illustrations became part of a larger *visual ecosystem.*

The challenge was finding the right balance. The illustrations needed to feel handcrafted without becoming rustic, artistic without becoming abstract, and contemporary without losing their warmth. Most importantly, they needed to remain *appetizing.*

What emerged was a flexible illustration system capable of generating countless combinations while maintaining a consistent visual identity. More than a set of assets, it became a <ref n="03"/> tool for *storytelling.*

annotations.text: The system was designed not only to decorate communication, but to help express the brand's values, products, and evolving narrative.

blocks.heading: READY, BUT NOT RELEASED

For all intents and purposes, the rebrand was ready.

*Which is where the story takes an unexpected turn. Because despite the work being complete, the project remains unpublished.*

As discussions expanded beyond design and into larger business considerations, investors and stakeholders arrived at a decision that was difficult, but understandable. The implementation would be paused until the timing aligned with broader business objectives and future growth plans.

And so the work waits.

Not because it isn't ready.

Not because anyone lost confidence in it.

Simply because timing matters.

blocks.leftColumn: *Designers often like to believe that good ideas succeed on the strength of the idea itself. *
blocks.rightColumn:
But brands exist within businesses, and businesses operate within realities that extend far beyond design. Market conditions, growth strategies, investments, and timing all influence when an idea enters the world.

Sometimes the most important decision is not what to launch.

It's when. The rebranding of Salad Days exists today as a complete system waiting patiently for its moment. The thinking is done. The work is done. The excitement remains very much alive.

blocks.heading:
*All that's left is time.*

And perhaps that was the most valuable lesson the project had to offer.

You can control the process. You can control the craft. You can control the execution.

*But the right time has a way of choosing itself.*

seo.metaTitle: You can control everything, but not the right time.
seo.metaDescription: After years of conversations, the Salad Days rebrand was ready to launch. This is the story of evolving a beloved brand and discovering that some ideas simply have to wait for their moment.
